**Why tulips were valued**

- **Novelty and rarity.** Tulips came from the Ottoman world and reached the Netherlands in the late 1500s. Wealthy collectors prized them as exotic.
- **Breaking.** The most coveted bulbs produced flames and feathers of color on the petals. We now know a virus caused this, which also weakened the plants and kept supply scarce. People at the time didn't know that, so the effect seemed almost miraculous. [Britannica covers the virus story.](https://www.britannica.com/story/tulip-mania-how-a-plant-virus-fueled-a-speculative-frenzy)
- **Status and wealth.** The Dutch Republic was very rich in the 1600s, and rare flowers were a way to show taste and money. Named varieties such as *Semper Augustus* became luxury goods.
- **Speculation.** In 1636–37, trading in contracts for bulbs still in the ground pushed prices up. Buyers expected to resell at a profit. Prices collapsed in early 1637. [Wikipedia's overview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania) summarizes this.

**Material from the period**

- **Satirical pamphlets.** *Samenspraeck tusschen Waermondt ende Gaergoedt* ("Conversation between Waermondt and Gaergoedt") was printed in Haarlem in 1637. It's a dialogue between a truthful man and a greedy one, and it mocks the trade. [A Christie's lot](https://www.christies.com.cn/lot/lot-6041138) lists a copy. [A UMass Dartmouth PDF](https://euro.sites.umassd.edu/files/2016/10/Tulipmania-Tulip-Speculation-and-Crash-1637.pdf) reproduces an English translation. I didn't check that translation against the Dutch original.
- **Tulip books.** Growers and dealers made watercolor catalogues of varieties. [The Norton Simon Museum](https://www.nortonsimon.org/art/detail/M.1974.08.030.D) has a *Semper Augustus* page from one. The [International Institute of Social History](https://archief.socialhistory.org/en/collections/tulip-mania) also has tulip mania material.

**Caveats**

- Most of the surviving written evidence comes from moralizing pamphlets written by critics. Price data from the time is thin and biased, and Wikipedia notes this.
- Reported prices for a single *Semper Augustus* bulb vary widely between sources, from a few thousand to over 10,000 guilders.
- Some modern historians think the "mania" was smaller than the legend says, because the crash may have hurt fewer people than the pamphlets suggest.
- The famous stories, such as a bulb traded for a house or eaten by a sailor mistaking it for an onion, come largely from Charles Mackay's 1841 book, not from the period.

Tibetan Buddhist texts describe meditation as a graded path. Different genres and lineages divide it differently, but a few frameworks recur.

## 1. Lamrim ("stages of the path") literature
- **Atiśa's *Lamp for the Path to Awakening*** (11th century) set the template. It organizes practice by three types of person: initial, middle, and advanced.
- **Tsongkhapa's *Lamrim Chenmo*** (c. 1402) is the classic elaboration. It places meditation inside a sequence: relying on a teacher, reflecting on precious human life, death and impermanence, karma, refuge, renunciation, bodhicitta, and then the six perfections.
- The last two perfections are **calm abiding (*śamatha*, Tib. *zhi gnas*)** and **special insight (*vipaśyanā*, Tib. *lhag mthong*)**.

## 2. Nine stages of calm abiding
Tibetan authors draw on Maitreya/Asaṅga's Indian sources and on Kamalaśīla. They describe nine mental states for developing stable concentration:
1. Placing the mind
2. Continuous placement
3. Patchwork (repeated) placement
4. Close placement
5. Taming
6. Pacifying
7. Thoroughly pacifying
8. One-pointedness
9. Balanced placement

- Teachers often illustrate the sequence with the **elephant, monkey, and rabbit** image. A monk leads an elephant, which stands for the mind, along a path. The elephant starts out black and gradually turns white.
- The text names five faults (such as laziness and forgetting the instruction) and eight antidotes.
- It also names the six powers and four types of attention that carry a practitioner through the stages.
- The result is **mental and physical pliancy** (*shin sbyangs*).

## 3. Kamalaśīla's *Stages of Meditation* (*Bhāvanākrama*)
Kamalaśīla was an 8th-century Indian master. He is traditionally said to have defeated the Chinese monk Heshang Moheyan at the "Council of Lhasa" (Samyé debate). The *Bhāvanākrama* became an authoritative Tibetan source for a gradual approach: compassion and bodhicitta first, then calm abiding, then insight into emptiness. It rejected a "sudden" approach with no preparation.

## 4. Tantric stages: generation and completion
- **Generation stage** (*bskyed rim*) is visualizing deities, mandalas, and pure appearances.
- **Completion stage** (*rdzogs rim*) works with subtle energy-channels, winds, and drops, as in the Six Yogas of Nāropa and the Kālacakra "six-limbed yoga".
- Mahāmudrā and Dzogchen add their own graded schemes. Mahāmudrā has the **four yogas** (one-pointedness, simplicity, one taste, non-meditation). Dzogchen has the "four visions" of Thögal.

## 5. The Five Paths
Across schools, the texts map these meditations onto the **five paths**: accumulation, preparation, seeing, meditation, and no more learning. These lead through the ten bodhisattva grounds (*bhūmi*) to buddhahood.

## Differences between schools
- **Gelug** stresses the analytical sequence of the lamrim and the union of calm abiding and insight.

**Hildegard of Bingen** (1098–1179), a 12th-century German Benedictine abbess, mystic, and polymath, was one of the earliest and most prolific medieval writers on natural science and herbal medicine. Her botanical and healing philosophies are primarily documented in two complementary treatises—originally composed together in the 1150s as *Liber subtilitatum diversarum naturarum creaturarum* (“Book on the Subtle Natures of Created Creatures”) and later divided into:

1. [***Physica***](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physica_(Hildegard)) (*Liber Simplicis Medicinae* / *Book of Simple Medicine*): An encyclopedic catalog of the natural world and the medicinal qualities of individual substances.
2. [***Causae et Curae***](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causae_et_Curae) (*Liber Compositae Medicinae* / *Causes and Cures*): A clinical treatise detailing etiology, human pathology, internal imbalances, and compound recipes for healing.

---

### 1. Key Theological and Philosophical Concepts

* ***Viriditas* ("Greening Power"):** 
  Central to Hildegard’s worldview is *viriditas*, the divine, life-giving vigor that permeates nature. To Hildegard, plants were the pure physical embodiment of this green vitality. When humans fell ill or experienced spiritual or physical exhaustion, plant remedies were used to transmit *viriditas* back into the body to revive and sustain it.
* **Humoral and Environmental Balance:** 
  Hildegard adapted classical Greco-Roman humoral theory (hot, cold, dry, moist). Rather than solely treating physical symptoms, she classified plants according to their elemental temperatures and subtle virtues to counteract internal bodily imbalances (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile).
* **Holistic Health (Microcosm and Macrocosm):** 
  She viewed the human body as a reflection of the larger cosmos. Healing required alignment among the physical body, the soul, nutrition, emotional state, and natural seasonal rhythms.

---

### 2. Botanical Writing in *Physica*

The first and largest section of *Physica* is devoted to plants and herbs (*De plantis*), accompanied by a separate section on trees (*De arboribus*). Together, they cover hundreds of species native to Central Europe. 

Rather than focusing on descriptive botany (how leaves or stems looked, assuming the practitioner already identified them), Hildegard focused on **practical application and therapeutic effects**:

* **Spelt (*Dinkel*):** Hildegard considered spelt the finest grain, describing it as warm, rich, easy to digest, and capable of generating "good blood" and a joyful spirit.
* **Fennel (*Fenichel*):** Highly praised as a restorative herb that dispels mucus, settles gastrointestinal distress, and brings pleasant breath and clear vision.
* **Wormwood (*Wermut*):** Recommended as a primary tonic and restorative elixir to combat fatigue, lung ailments, and melancholy.
* **Galangal and Bertram (Pellitory-of-the-wall):** Warming spices and roots prescribed to strengthen digestion, improve nutrient absorption, and protect against fever and weakness.

---

### 3. Practical Therapeutics and Preparation

In *Causae et Curae*, Hildegard outlined how to transform these plants into effective treatments:

* **Preparation Methods:** Plants were prepared as decoctions, teas, infused herbal wines, tinctures, powders, vinegars, and topical salves or poultices.
* **Dietary Medicine:** She viewed daily food as the first line of healing, arguing that improper diet caused toxic humors to accumulate, while simple, wholesome plant-based foods restored balance.
* **Head-to-Toe Remedies:** Her texts organized treatments systematically across the body—treating everything from headaches and eye problems to gastrointestinal distress, respiratory congestion, and joint pains.

---

### Legacy

Hildegard's writings represent a unique synthesis of monastic garden practice, regional German folk herbalism, and theological cosmology. In the 20th and 21st centuries, her writings sparked a major resurgence known as *Hildegard-Medizin* (monastic phytotherapy), and she is widely celebrated as one of Western history's earliest documented female medical writers.

During the Dutch Golden Age of the 1630s, tulips became prized luxury goods and speculative assets. The valuation of tulips—and the eventual speculative frenzy known as **Tulip Mania** (*tulpenmanie*)—stemmed from a combination of aesthetics, biology, social status, and financial mechanisms:

---

### Why People Thought Tulips Were Valuable

1. **Exotic Novelty and Saturated Colors**
   * Tulips were brought to Western Europe from the Ottoman Empire in the late 16th century, famously planted and propagated by botanist Carolus Clusius at Leiden University.
   * Unlike the native wildflowers known to Western Europe, tulips offered intense, deeply saturated tones (vivid reds, purples, yellows, and pure whites) and bloomed early in spring.

2. **The Mystery of "Broken" Petals (Mosaic Virus)**
   * The most expensive and sought-after varieties were not solid in color, but "broken"—featuring intricate feathering and flame-like streaks (such as the famous *Semper Augustus* and *Viceroy*).
   * 17th-century botanists could not explain or reliably predict these mutations. Today we know they were caused by the aphid-borne **tulip breaking virus**, which weakened the bulb and made reproduction slow and difficult. Because they could not be bred on demand, bulbs producing broken patterns were exceptionally rare status symbols.

3. **Status and Conspicuous Consumption in the Dutch Republic**
   * As trade flourished, the Dutch Republic produced an affluent merchant and regent class. Wealthy burghers collected curiosities, paintings, rare plants, and exotic items to display their refined taste and social standing. Having a garden with rare tulips became an unmistakable marker of prestige.

4. **Biological Rhythm and the Creation of Futures Contracts**
   * Tulips only bloom in spring and can only be safely unearthed, transported, and replanted while dormant during the summer (June through September).
   * To trade year-round, Dutch merchants developed forward contracts in taverns (*colleges*). Buyers and sellers signed notarized agreements to exchange bulbs months later. This made tulip trading liquid and detached from physical plants, attracting speculators who never intended to plant the flowers, only to resell the paper contracts at a markup.

---

### Contemporary Sources and Evidence from the Period (1630s)

A wealth of primary documentation survives from the 17th century detailing the market and public reaction:

* **The Dialogue of Waermondt and Gaergoedt (1636–1637):**
  * One of the most famous contemporary pamphlets was [*Samen-spraeck tusschen Waermondt ende Gaergoedt*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania) (*Dialogue between True-Mouth and Covet-Good*). Written anonymously in Dutch, it dramatized how ordinary artisans and weavers were abandoning their trades to bet fortunes on paper contracts.
* **The "Discovery of Folly" Pamphlets & Commodity Trade Lists (1636–1637):**
  * Period pamphlets aimed at cautioning against the speculation published itemized comparisons illustrating what a single *Viceroy* bulb contract cost at peak prices (roughly 2,500 to 3,000 guilders), equating it to:
    * *Two lasts of wheat, four lasts of rye, four fat oxen, eight pigs, twelve sheep, two hogsheads of wine, four tuns of beer, a thousand pounds of cheese, a bed, a suit of clothes, and a silver cup.*
* **Pieter Cos's Tulip Book (*Verzameling van een Meenigte Tulipaanen*, 1637):**
  * Florist catalogues and illustrated tulip albums (like the 1637 [Pieter Cos manuscript](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania)) survive today. These watercolored florilegia recorded the weight in *azen* (a tiny fraction of a gram) and the soaring guilder prices of named varieties right before the market collapsed in February 1637.
* **17th-Century Satirical Art:**
  * Following the collapse, artists produced moralizing satires, most notably Jan Brueghel the Younger's painting [*A Satire of Tulip Mania*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania) (c. 1640), depicting speculators as foolishly dressed monkeys trading bulbs, writing receipts, and being hauled before magistrates.
* **Notarial and Court Archives:**
  * City archives in Haarlem, Amsterdam, and Alkmaar preserve notarial acts, contracts, and municipal resolutions. Modern historical research by scholar [Anne Goldgar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania) in Dutch archives demonstrated that while prices soared into thousands of guilders, the trades were largely concentrated within tight networks of affluent connoisseurs and merchants rather than causing the nationwide economic ruin depicted by later Victorian retellings.

Tibetan Buddhist literature provides highly detailed, systematic maps of meditation. The most influential frameworks come from foundational Indian treatises translated into Tibetan—principally Kamalaśīla’s [*Bhāvanākrama*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bh%C4%81van%C4%81krama) (*Stages of Meditation*) and Asaṅga’s [*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yogacarabhumi-sastra)—which were subsequently synthesized in Tibetan manuals like Je Tsongkhapa’s [*Lamrim Chenmo*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamrim) (*The Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path to Enlightenment*).

Tibetan texts generally divide meditation into an **overarching path** (from motivation to insight) and a **micro-progression of attentional training** (the Nine Stages of Settling the Mind).

---

### 1. The Overarching Stages of Meditation
In treatises such as Kamalaśīla’s [*Bhāvanākrama*](https://www.scribd.com/document/518663801/Bhavanakrama-Stages-of-Meditation), meditation unfolds across four broad phases:

1. **Foundational Motivation (*Bodhicitta* and Compassion):** Before cultivating deep absorption, the practitioner develops great compassion (*karuṇā*) and the aspiration to attain enlightenment for the benefit of all beings.
2. **Calm Abiding (*Śamatha*):** Cultivating stable, single-pointed concentration to subdue mental turbulence, sensory distraction, and dullness.
3. **Special Insight (*Vipaśyanā*):** Once the mind is calm and pliant, analytical meditation is applied to investigate the nature of phenomena and realize emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
4. **Union of *Śamatha* and *Vipaśyanā* (*Yuganaddha*): The seamless synthesis of sustained mental stillness and penetrating analytical insight, cutting the root of cyclic existence.

---

### 2. The Nine Stages of Settling the Mind (*Navākāra-citta-sthiti*)
To achieve *Śamatha*, texts codified in the [Study Buddhism / Berzin Archives](https://studybuddhism.com/en/advanced-studies/science-of-mind/concentration/the-nine-stages-of-settling-the-mind) outline nine specific psychological stages. These describe how a meditator transitions from intense mental agitation to effortless concentration:

#### Phase I: Overcoming Gross Distraction (Developing Stability)
* **1. Setting the Mind (*Cittasthāpana*):** Placing attention on the focal object (e.g., the breath or an image of the Buddha). Distractions are constant, and the mind resembles a turbulent waterfall.
* **2. Setting with Continuity (*Saṁsthāpana*):** Attention remains on the object for brief intervals before wandering. The meditator experiences occasional moments of stillness.
* **3. Resetting (*Upasthāpana*):** Mindfulness (*smṛti*) strengthens, allowing the meditator to quickly notice when attention has drifted and bring it back without falling into protracted daydreaming.
* **4. Closely Setting (*Prasthāpana*):** The power of mindfulness prevents the mind from completely losing the object during the session, though subtle distractions still flutter in the background.

#### Phase II: Overcoming Subtle Dullness (Developing Clarity)
* **5. Taming the Mind (*Damana*):** By contemplating the benefits of concentration, the practitioner experiences joy and prevents wandering. However, the mind faces the hazard of subtle dullness or mental sluggishness (*laya*).
* **6. Stilling the Mind (*Śamana*):** The meditator sharpens vigilance (*samprajañya*) to detect and pacify subtle dullness and low energy, restoring clarity.
* **7. Completely Stilling (*Vyupaśamana*):** Subtle agitation or sluggishness are eliminated as soon as they emerge, requiring only slight vigilance to maintain focus.

#### Phase III: Effortless Stability (Mastery)
* **8. Single-Pointedness (*Ekagratākaraṇa*):** Concentration proceeds smoothly for long stretches with only an initial application of effort at the start of the session.
* **9. Absorbed / Balanced Setting (*Samāhita*):** Full mastery is attained. Concentration becomes spontaneous, sustained, and completely effortless (*anābhoga*).

---

### 3. The Climax: Mental and Physical Pliability (*Praśrabdhi*)
Texts note that completing the ninth stage is not yet the full attainment of *Śamatha*. The final transition occurs when prolonged concentration induces a state of **mental and physical pliancy/suppleness** (*shinjang* / *praśrabdhi*)—an energetic lightness and bliss in body and mind that frees the meditator from fatigue and makes the mind an exceptionally flexible instrument for insight meditation (*Vipaśyanā*).

Teaching what Machiavelli’s contemporaries thought of him is an effective way to dismantle the modern cartoon caricature of the ruthless schemer and reveal the nuanced reality of Renaissance politics. 

A central tension to highlight for your class is the contrast between **the man his peers personally knew** and **the explosive reaction to his writings** as they began to circulate.

---

### 1. As a Person and Friend: Warm, Witty, and Liked
In popular culture, Machiavelli is often imagined as a humorless, sinister plotter. For those who lived with and worked alongside him, he was anything but:
* **The Charismatic Intellectual:** Machiavelli was renowned for his biting wit, conversational charm, and love of storytelling. He wrote one of the most successful Renaissance stage comedies of his era, [*Mandragola*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mandrake), which earned him wide acclaim as a dramatist and literary figure.
* **Warm Friendships:** His personal correspondence—most famously with prominent Florentine diplomats and historians like [Francesco Vettori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Vettori) and [Francesco Guicciardini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Guicciardini)—reveals lively camaraderie. They gossiped, joked about romance, debated Roman history, and shared mutual affection. Guicciardini considered him a dear friend and intellectual peer, even while critiquing some of his bolder ideas.

---

### 2. As a Politician and Diplomat: An Ardent Republican Patriot
To the citizens and leaders of Florence, Machiavelli was seen not as a servant of autocrats, but as a dedicated public servant of the Florentine Republic:
* **Devotion to the Republic:** For 14 years (1498–1512), Machiavelli served as the Secretary to the Second Chancery of Florence, handling foreign diplomacy and organizing a local citizen-militia to reduce reliance on corrupt mercenaries (detailed in the [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Niccolò Machiavelli](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/machiavelli/)).
* **Target of the Medici:** When the Medici family dismantled the republic and returned to power in 1512, Machiavelli was viewed as a political opponent. He was dismissed from office, imprisoned, and subjected to torture under suspicion of plotting against the Medici, before being exiled to his country estate. His contemporaries knew him as someone who had suffered directly for his republican commitments.

---

### 3. As a Political Thinker: The Shock of "The Effective Truth"
During his lifetime, *The Prince* was not widely published as a book; it circulated in manuscript form among a closed network of humanist intellectuals and patrons (formal publication came posthumously in 1532):
* **The Break with Humanist "Mirror-for-Princes":** Previous Renaissance treatises taught that rulers should model Christian virtues—clemency, piety, honesty, and justice. When contemporaries read Machiavelli's assertion that a ruler must know how *“to be able not to be good”* when necessity demands, the reaction was genuine shock. 
* **Guicciardini’s Critique:** Machiavelli’s close contemporary and critic Francesco Guicciardini wrote [Considerations on the Discourses of Machiavelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Guicciardini). While Guicciardini shared Machiavelli's realistic appraisal of power, he criticized Machiavelli for being too rigid, drawing sweeping generalizations from ancient Roman examples, and taking an excessive delight in extreme, scandalous measures.
* **Suspicion from Both Sides:** Later in life, when Machiavelli tried to re-enter civic service, he found himself politically distrusted by both factions:
  * The **Medici** remained suspicious of his lifelong republican sympathies.
  * The **Republicans** (especially after the Medici were briefly expelled again in 1527) mistrusted him because he had dedicated *The Prince* to Lorenzo de' Medici and accepted commissions from Pope Clement VII.

---

### 4. The Immediate Posthumous Reception: The Birth of "Old Nick"
Shortly after his death in 1527 and the printing of his major works in 1532, the public perception curdled rapidly across Europe:
* **Condemnation by the Church:** Moralists and the Catholic Church condemned his work as an assault on Christian ethics. In 1559, Pope Paul IV placed all of Machiavelli's writings on the papal [*Index of Prohibited Books*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Index_Librorum_Prohibitorum).
* **The "Teacher of Evil":** Early commentators accused him of writing handbooks for tyrannical manipulation, cementing the pejorative label "Machiavellian" and linking his first name (*Niccolò*) in English popular folklore to the devil (*"Old Nick"*).

---

### Discussion Prompts for Your Class
1. **The Paradox of Loyalty:** *Why did contemporaries in 1527 mistrust Machiavelli for serving the Medici, even though he wrote the intensely republican Discourses on Livy and was tortured by the Medici in 1513?*
2. **Intent vs. Reception:** *Did Machiavelli write The Prince to educate a tyrant, or to expose the brutal reality of how princes operate to an unsuspecting public?* (A theory famously proposed later by Jean-Jacques Rousseau).

## Framing for the class
"Contemporaries" covers two groups:
1. **People who knew him** (died 1527). They judged Machiavelli the man: a colleague, friend, rival or client.
2. **The first readers of his books.** *The Prince* wasn't printed until 1532, so the hostile reaction came mostly after his death.

Scholars note that [the work circulated from 1513 but wasn't published until 1532, and that early period is less studied](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/review-of-politics/article/five-hundred-years-of-italian-scholarship-on-machiavellis-prince/F71AC0E70B26DB3F650FD97B6BB7FF1B). That gap makes a good discussion point. Most of the "Machiavellian" villain image was built by people who never met him.

## What the sources support
- **Francesco Vettori (friend and correspondent):** The 1513 letters between the two are [the key source for how Machiavelli tested his ideas on a peer](https://cambridge.org/core/journals/renaissance-quarterly/article/machiavelli-and-soderini/F529090745A6B9244447B5281C58A51A) while he was writing *The Prince*. Vettori treated him as a sharp, valued interlocutor, though not always as an authority.
- **Guicciardini:** Felix Gilbert's study [*Machiavelli and Guicciardini*](https://bard.edu/library/pdfs/archives/2024/08/Gilbert-Machiavelli_Guicciardini.pdf) is the standard comparison of the two. From my background knowledge, Guicciardini was a close friend, but in his *Considerations on the Discourses* he criticized Machiavelli for being too schematic and too fond of sweeping rules.
- **Soderini:** Bertelli's article [Machiavelli and Soderini](https://cambridge.org/core/journals/renaissance-quarterly/article/machiavelli-and-soderini/F529090745A6B9244447B5281C58A51A) covers the relationship with the gonfaloniere Machiavelli served. After the Medici returned in 1512, Machiavelli was tainted by his association with Soderini.
- **Wider circle:** Simonetta Machiavelli's [*All Machiavelli's Men*](https://www.newitalianbooks.it/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/Simonetta-Machiavelli-Proposal-ENGLISH.pdf) presents him through the eyes of friends, rivals, colleagues and enemies. It could be a useful resource for you.
- **Split early reception:** Some readers took *The Prince* as a [frank, sometimes ironic description of the evil means used by bad rulers, others as a set of evil recommendations to tyrants](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/review-of-politics/article/five-hundred-years-of-italian-scholarship-on-machiavellis-prince/F71AC0E70B26DB3F650FD97B6BB7FF1B). It was [well received when printed in 1532, and an anti-Machiavellian movement formed by mid-century](https://www.ssoar.info/ssoar/handle/document/61914).
- **Cardinal Pole (posthumous):** In his 1539 *Apologia ad Carolum Quintum*, Pole [called the book "written by an enemy of the human race"](https://doi.org/10.1353/sor.2014.0006). Pole also claimed Florentines told him Machiavelli wrote it to please a tyrant. Pole never knew Machiavelli, so he works better as the start of the legend than as a contemporary opinion.
- **Theological condemnation:** [Ambrogio Catarino Politi's *De libris a christiano detestandis* (Rome, 1552)](https://publires.unicatt.it/en/publications/machiavello-defuit-pietas-ovvero-le-macchie-del-machiavello-linte-9/) is the earliest Politi source I found. The line of condemnation runs on to the Jesuit Antonio Possevino in the early 1590s.

## From my background knowledge (verify first)
- Machiavelli was tortured on the strappado in 1513 over suspected involvement in an anti-Medici plot, then released. Later the Medici gave him a commission to write the *Florentine Histories*, so he wasn't a pariah.
- His friend Biagio Buonaccorsi wrote to him in a teasing, familiar tone. This shows he was seen as witty and sociable, not as a sinister figure.
- Machiavelli's comedy *La Mandragola* was a hit, and many contemporaries knew him mainly as a playwright and writer.
- Agostino Nifo's 1523 *De regnandi peritia* is often said to borrow heavily from *The Prince*, which suggests some readers took the ideas seriously and quietly.

## Classroom ideas
- **Source comparison:** Give students Machiavelli's letter to Vettori (10 Dec 1513), a Guicciardini passage, and Pole's *Apologia*. Ask which describes the man and which describes a reputation.
- **Debate:** Was *The Prince* satire, advice or a job application to the Medici?
- **Timeline:** Plot 1513 (writing), 1527 (death), 1532 (printing), 1539 (Pole) and 1552 (Politi) to show how the reputation changed.

### 1. The Classic English Translation & Adaptation: Edward Topsell (1607 / 1658)
In 1607, the English clergyman Edward Topsell published ***The Historie of Foure-Footed Beastes*** (later reissued in 1658 alongside his work on serpents as *The History of Four-Footed Beasts and Serpents*). 
* Topsell’s text is essentially a direct English translation, compilation, and adaptation of Gessner’s *Liber I: De Quadrupedibus Viviparis*, retaining most of Gessner’s animal accounts, woodcut illustrations, and classical references (with some added moral commentary).
* **Where to read it online:**

---

### 2. Digital Humanities & Machine-Assisted Modern Translations
* **Zenodo Open-Access Repositories:** Several digital humanities and source-text preservation projects have created digitized and automated English translations of Gessner’s Latin text. Full-text drafts and machine-assisted modern English translations of *Historiae Animalium Liber I* have been published on the open-access research repository [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org).

### 3. Original Latin Text & Illustrations
If you want to consult the original 1551 Latin edition alongside the English adaptations:
* **Biodiversity Heritage Library (BHL) / Internet Archive:** High-resolution scans of the 1551 Zurich edition (*Christoph Froschauer*) are freely accessible on the [Biodiversity Heritage Library / Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/conradigesnerime00gesn).

### Is there an English translation?

**No complete, official English translation exists** for *Thesaurus Exorcismorum Atque Conjurationum Terribilium* (either Part 2 or the compendium as a whole). 

* **The Work's Nature:** Compiled in 1608 by Lazarus Zetzner, the *Thesaurus Exorcismorum* is a massive (~1,300-page) early modern Latin omnibus collecting major 16th-century exorcism manuals by Franciscan demonologists, including:
  * **Valerio Polidoro** (*Practica Exorcistarum* & *Dispersio Daemonum*)
  * **Girolamo Menghi** (*Flagellum Daemonum* & *Fustis Daemonum*)
  * **Zacharia Visconti** (*Complementum Artis Exorcisticae*)
  * **Pietro Antonio Stampa** (*Fuga Satanae*)
* **Translation Status:** Because it served as a specialized Latin reference compendium for Catholic clergy, the overarching compendium has never been published in a complete, standard English edition. 
* **Partial / Standalone Translations:** Individual treatises that make up sections of the compendium—specifically Girolamo Menghi's works (*Flagellum Daemonum* / *Fustis Daemonum*)—have occasionally been translated or excerpted into English by academic scholars and independent specialty publishers (for example, [The Thinking Press edition of *The Cudgel of Demons*](https://www.thethinkingpress.org/product-page/the-cudgel-of-demons-fustis-daemonum-by-girolamo-menghi-series-c)). However, no comprehensive, open-access English edition of the entire multi-author compendium is available online.

---

### Where can you read it online?

While a complete English translation is not available, full, high-resolution digitized facsimiles of the original Latin texts can be browsed and downloaded freely from European digital archives:

* **[Wellcome Collection](https://wellcomecollection.org/works/a4dzzx9n):** Holds and provides a free, high-resolution digital viewer and PDF download of the 1608 Cologne edition.
* **[Münchener DigitalisierungsZentrum / Bavarian State Library (BSB)](https://www.digitale-sammlungen.de/):** Hosts digitized scans of the 1608 and 1626 editions.
* **[Internet Archive](https://archive.org/):** Hosts various digitized historical editions and related 16th/17th-century demonological texts by Menghi, Polidoro, and Visconti.

### Language & Availability Details

* **Original Format:** The work is strictly a **Yucatec Maya to Spanish** dictionary, compiled by Juan Pío Pérez and published posthumously between 1866 and 1877 in Mérida, Yucatán.

### English Alternatives and Combined Databases

If you need to consult Pío Pérez's lexical data in English, researchers rely on integrated dictionaries and databases that incorporate his entries:

1. **David Bolles' Combined Dictionary–Concordance:**
   * David Bolles compiled historical colonial and 19th-century Yucatec Maya sources—including Juan Pío Pérez (*JPP*), the *Calepino Maya de Motul*, and the *Diccionario de San Francisco*—into standardized databases with English cross-references.
   * You can consult these reports and dictionary files hosted online via the [Foundation for the Advancement of Mesoamerican Studies, Inc. (FAMSI)](http://www.famsi.org/reports/96072/index.html) and [David's Books / Maya Studies](https://davidsbooks.org/).
2. **Modern Mayan–English Dictionaries:**
   * For English translations of Yucatec Maya terms, modern linguistic works such as Victoria Bricker, Eleuterio Poot Yah, and Ofelia Dzul de Po'ot's *A Dictionary of the Maya Language As Spoken in Hocabá, Yucatán* (University of Utah Press) serve as direct Maya–English references.

### English Title and Background
Jacob Aertsz. Colom originally published his seminal Dutch maritime pilot guide and sea atlas as ***De Vyerighe Colom*** (1632) and later in an expanded folio edition titled ***De groote lichtende ofte vyerighe colom over de zee-custen van 't Wester, Ooster, en Noorder vaer-water*** (c. 1651). 

To cater to English navigators and international shipping, Colom and contemporary Amsterdam publishers translated and issued his guide in English under slightly varying titles:
* ***The Fierie Sea-Columne*** (or *The New Fierie Sea-Columne*), first issued in the 1630s and 1640s (e.g., subtitled *"Wherein Are shewed the Seas, and Sea-coasts of the Northern, Eastern, and Western Navigation..."*).
* ***The Lighting Colomne, or Sea-Mirrour*** (or *The Lightning Columne*), published in subsequent editions throughout the mid-to-late 17th century by Colom and later continued by publishers such as Jacob and Casparus Lootsman.

### Background and Context
* **The Original Work:** First published in Venice by the Aldine Press in 1542 (and subsequently expanded into multi-volume editions in years such as 1554 and 1564), the anthology is a massive collection of 16th-century vernacular Italian letters (*letteratura epistolare*) by notable humanists, poets, religious figures, and statesmen (such as Pietro Bembo, Claudio Tolomei, and Annibal Caro). 
* **Partial / Scholarly Translations:** While the complete multi-volume anthology has never been translated as a unified work, individual letters or short selections are occasionally translated and cited in specialized English-language academic books and journals (for instance, studies on the Aldine Press, Italian epistolary culture, or Renaissance religious history found on platforms like [Cambridge Core](https://www.cambridge.org/) and [JSTOR](https://www.jstor.org/)).

### Where to Read the Original Italian Online
If you can read early modern Italian or wish to run sections through modern machine translation tools, digitizations of original 16th-century Aldine printings are freely accessible:
* Multiple copies and volumes of the 16th-century printings can be viewed and downloaded on the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/search?query=%22lettere+volgari+di+diversi%22).
* High-resolution digital scans are also accessible via the [HathiTrust Digital Library](https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Search/Home?lookfor=%22lettere+volgari+di+diversi%22&searchtype=all) and [Google Books](https://books.google.com/).

**No complete English translation** of Johann Rudolf Wyss’s *Reise in das Berner Oberland* (Volume 1 or 2) was ever published or exists in standard library catalogs. 

### Publication & Translation History
* **Original Work:** Published in Bern by J. J. Burgdorfer in two parts (Volume 1 in 1816, Volume 2 in 1817), this work served as an influential topographical, folkloric, and travel account of the Bernese Alps (documented on [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Rudolf_Wyss)).
* **Historical Translations:** While an early contemporary French translation was produced in 1817 by Henri-Antoine de Crousaz-Meyn (*Voyage dans l'Oberland bernois*), no full English edition was printed during the 19th-century Alpine travel boom or in modern commercial publication.

### Is There an English Translation?

**Strictly speaking, the original work titled *"Aristophanis Comoediae"* edited by Wilhelm Dindorf is not in English.** Dindorf's editions (such as the Oxford edition and the Didot Paris bilingual edition titled *Aristophanis Comoediae et deperditarum fragmenta... Graece et latine*) contain the ancient Greek text accompanied by Latin translations, Latin annotations, and scholarly apparatus.

However, because Wilhelm Dindorf’s recension became the standard critical edition in the 19th century, **direct English translations based specifically on Dindorf’s revised text were produced.**

The most notable and complete direct translation is:
* **_The Comedies of Aristophanes: A New and Literal Translation from the Revised Text of Dindorf_** by **William James Hickie** (published by Henry G. Bohn / George Bell & Sons).

### Why It Has Not Been Translated
Frischlin’s work is a specialized 16th-century Neo-Latin pedagogical manual and grammatical treatise that compiles Latin grammatical rules and critiques earlier medieval and Renaissance grammarians. Because of its niche academic nature and substantial length, it has remained untranslated into English by modern scholars, though it remains a subject of study in historical linguistics and Renaissance humanism (see his biographical entry in the [Deutsche Biographie](https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/sfz17646.html)).

---

### Background of the Work

***Der flammende Stern, oder die Gesellschaft der Freymäurer: von allen Seiten betrachtet*** (Berlin, 1779) is the 18th-century German translation of the original French work by **Théodore-Henri, Baron de Tschoudy**: ***L'Étoile flamboyante, ou La société des francs-maçons, considérée sous tous les aspects*** (published in two volumes in 1766). 

---

### Is there a complete English translation?

* **No complete, official English edition of the entire two-volume work has been published in standard commercial print.** 
* However, **its most famous and influential section—the Hermetic-Masonic Catechism** (*Instruction des Philosophes Inconnus* / *The Catechism of the Burning or Blazing Star*)—was translated into English by Arthur Edward Waite and other esoteric researchers. Waite included it under the title *A Short Catechism of Alchemy* (or *Paracelsus' Alchemical Catechism*) in his compilation *The Hermetic and Alchemical Writings of Paracelsus*, and it has also circulated independently.

---

**No, there is no published English translation** of *“La sabiduria universal del B. Raymundo Lullio propuesta en panegyrico discurso…”* by Bartolomé Antonio Fullana (Bartholomeus Antonius Fullana).

---

### Background
* **Nature of the Work:** It is a 1712 Spanish panegyric discourse (a formal sermon/oratorical praise) delivered by the Jesuit priest Bartolomé Antonio Fullana on January 25, 1712, celebrating the philosopher and mystic Ramon Llull (*Raymundo Lulio*) as patron of the Literary University of the Kingdom of Mallorca.
* **Publication History:** It was printed in Mallorca by Miguel Capó in 1712 and remains an obscure 18th-century academic/religious pamphlet without modern English translations.

---

### Where to Read the Original Spanish Online
You can read and consult digital reproductions of the original 1712 edition free of charge through historical repository collections:

* **[Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes](https://www.cervantesvirtual.com/obra/la-sabiduria-universal-del-b-raymundo-lullio-propuesta-en-panegyrico-discurso-en-la-solemne-fiesta-que-como-a-su-patron-le-consagro-la-universidad-literaria-del-reyno-de-mallorca-dia-25-de-enero-1712/)** – Holds the digitized copy from the University of Barcelona (CRAI Fons Antic).
* **[Google Books](https://books.google.com/books?id=f_U9AAAAcAAJ)** – Digital scan of the original 1712 imprint from the Biblioteca de Catalunya / University of Barcelona collections.

### Is There an English Translation?

**Yes.** R. Campbell Thompson published his work on Gilgamesh in two related companion volumes:

1. ***The Epic of Gilgamish: Text, Transliteration, and Notes*** (Oxford University Press / Clarendon Press, 1930) is the critical scholarly edition. It primarily contains the Akkadian cuneiform text plates, transliterations, critical apparatus, and philological notes rather than an English prose/verse narrative translation.
2. ***The Epic of Gilgamish: A New Translation*** (Luzac & Co., 1928) is Thompson’s accompanying full English translation (*"rendered literally into English hexameters from a collation of the cuneiform tablets in the British Museum"*). 

---

### Where to Read It Online

You can access both Thompson’s translation and his critical edition through several online repositories:

* **[Internet Sacred Text Archive (sacred-texts.com)](https://www.sacred-texts.com/ane/eog/index.htm):** Hosts the complete, transcribed HTML text of Thompson's 1928 English translation, broken down into twelve tablets.
* **[Internet Archive (archive.org)](https://archive.org/details/epicofgilgamishn0000regi):** Contains scanned digital facsimiles and downloadable PDFs of Thompson's [1928 translation](https://archive.org/details/thompson-1928-gilgamesh), as well as related digitized materials from British Museum Assyriology collections.
* **[Global Grey Ebooks](https://www.globalgreyebooks.com/the-epic-of-gilgamish.html):** Offers free formatted digital editions (PDF, EPUB, online text) of the 1928 English translation.
* **[HathiTrust Digital Library](https://catalog.hathitrust.org/):** Catalogs and provides digital search and institutional access to the 1930 Clarendon Press edition (*Text, Transliteration, and Notes*).
* **[Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI)](https://cdli.earth/):** Provides digital metadata, fragment images, and transliterations referencing Thompson's 1930 plate and line numbering system.

### Is There an English Translation?

**No complete, published English translation exists** for Volume 60 (卷六十) of the *Wubei Zhi* (*Treatise on Armaments and Military Provisions*, 武備志), compiled by Mao Yuanyi (茅元儀) in 1621.

Due to the monumental size of the *Wubei Zhi*—spanning 240 volumes (*juan*) and more than two million characters—only selected sections have ever been translated into English. These translations are largely confined to:
* Specific martial arts treatises (such as the sword and saber manuals or Qi Jiguang’s fist methods, discussed on platforms like [Kung Fu Tea](https://chinesemartialstudies.com/)).
* The Zheng He navigation chart in Volume 240.

Volume 60 belongs to the section **《陣練制·陣九》** (*Zhen Lian Zhi* – Formations and Training, Part 9), which focuses on classical battle array diagrams and tactical theory (specifically adaptations of Zhuge Liang and Tang general Li Jing's "Eight Formations"). Aside from potential brief quotes or analyses in specialized academic papers on Chinese military history, it has not been systematically translated into English.

---

### Where to Access the Text Online

While a full English translation is unavailable, you can read the original Chinese text along with high-resolution historical scans online:

* **[Chinese Text Project (CText) – Wubei Zhi](https://ctext.org/wiki.pl?if=en&res=878696):**
  CText hosts scanned fascicles and digitized text. Volume 60 is cataloged within the volume group covering volumes 59–60 (`二十八 v59~60`).
* **[Library of Congress – Wubei Zhi Collection](https://www.loc.gov/item/2021666687/):**
  The Library of Congress provides open-access, complete high-resolution digital scans of original Ming-dynasty woodblock editions of the work.
